newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals -- Cobalt climbs amid Zaire turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals -- Cobalt climbs amid Zaire turmoil.

text.p: Cobalt prices continued their recent climb as uncertainties over supplies from Zaire and the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency tender encouraged bulls in the market, Asian traders said on Tuesday.
"The situation in Zaire and the delay in the DLA tender are adding to uncertainties," said one trader at a major trading house. "Prices are heading towards $25 (a lb) and higher."
Asian traders said high-grade cobalt had risen to $24.00/24.50 a lb, pushing up lower-grade Russian metal to $22.50/23.00.

On Monday, major producer Gecamines closed its headquarters in Lubumbashi as Zaire rebels advanced on the city. Despite peace talks in South Africa, rebels continued their advance into Zaire's mineral rich region of Shaba. Explosions were reported overnight on approaches to Lubumbashi.
In the United States, the Defense National Stockpile said on Monday the opening of bids for cobalt, originally scheduled for April 7, was to be delayed until further notice.

The trader said Zaire suspended April shipments after completing March deliveries. Some other major suppliers such as Inco Ltd and Sherritt International Corp of Canada also stopped delivery in hopes for higher prices, he added.

China's Xinhua news agency said on Tuesday China had begun construction of a production line for cobalt oxide in the southern province of Hainan, which should produce 200 tonnes a year after completion.
Antimony prices in China continued to edge up and traders reported receiving firm Chinese offers for antimony ingots at levels above $2,475 per tonne, CIF Rotterdam.
"I think the price of antimony ingots will be even higher in a few weeks," said one trader, adding it could reach a high of $3,000 per tonne.
Some antimony had been traded at $2,470 per tonne, another source said, but no further details were available.
State-run trader China National Import Export Corp (CNIEC) had cracked down on antimony smuggling and at the moment only CNIEC was offering antimony on the market, one trader said.
"Supplies are pretty tight," he said.
Japan's molybdenum oxide market was steady at $4.60/70 a lb, with many participants holding to the sidelines to see which way prices were heading.

One trader said the market was divided over the future direction of prices and was waiting for more information about shipments from Molycorp of the United States and about demand, particularly from the car industry.
The magnesium market was flat, but some traders said sentiment was firm amid rising production costs in China.
"Prices might rise gradually by $100 to $200 (a tonne) by the end of this year," one trader said.
